data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["RFC 9110 defines these terms for HTTP request methods specifically; the event-log writer is not an HTTP method in general","RFC 9110 idempotence is about 'intended effect on the server,' a semantic/declarative notion, whereas event-log idempotence is typically enforced mechanically via deduplication keys","HTTP safety includes a client-expectation component (the client does not expect state change); event-log writers always expect state change"],"overturn_conditions":["If RFC 9110 text does not actually establish safe \u2282 idempotent (e.g., if safe and idempotent are defined independently without stated subset relation), the hierarchy claim must be weakened","If RFC 9110 defines idempotence over response equality only and not server-state equality, the mapping to event-log deduplication breaks"],"shared_structure":["Both safe and idempotent are properties of operation repetition behavior","Safe is a strictly stronger property: all safe operations are idempotent (a no-op repeated is still a no-op), but not all idempotent operations are safe (PUT and DELETE mutate state but converge under repetition)","The event-log writer's append operation maps to the idempotent-but-not-safe quadrant"],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_005","SRC_006"],"transfer_claims":["The set-inclusion hierarchy (safe \u2282 idempotent) transfers: an operation that never mutates state is trivially idempotent, so any writer that were safe would also be idempotent, but safety is too strong for append operations","The 'same effect under repetition' notion transfers from HTTP idempotence to the event-log writer's deduplication requirement"]},"claim":"Per RFC 9110, a safe method is one whose semantics are essentially read-only (no server state change is intended or expected), while an idempotent method is one where multiple identical requests have the same intended server effect as a single request. The distinction is that safe forbids side effects entirely, whereas idempotent permits side effects but requires them to converge. An append-only event log with at-least-once delivery requires idempotence of its writers \u2014 not safety \u2014 because appending an event is inherently state-changing (not read-only), yet a retried append must not duplicate the event.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If RFC 9110 \u00a79.2 defines idempotence purely over HTTP response equality rather than server-state equality, the transfer to event-log semantics would be weakened because the log cares about deduplicated state, not HTTP responses.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the event log's delivery model were exactly-once rather than at-least-once, idempotence would not be required of writers because no retries would occur.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the append-only log is defined such that duplicate physical appends are acceptable (deduplication performed at read time), then writers need neither safety nor idempotence \u2014 downstream consumers would bear the burden.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Safety constrains the effect class (no mutation). Idempotence constrains the effect's behavior under repetition (mutation is allowed but must be invariant under duplication). In an append-only log, writers mutate state (append), so safety is impossible; but at-least-once delivery guarantees retries, so without idempotence each retry would append a duplicate, corrupting the log. Idempotent writers \u2014 typically via client-assigned sequence numbers or idempotency keys \u2014 ensure the second append of the same logical event is a no-op.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
